title: 🎙️ Science, Wonder & the Natural World
description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. We're after stories that inspire curiosity and wonder about how the world works. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. We're after stories that inspire curiosity and wonder about how the world works.
_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Science, Wonder & the Natural World' — scientific discovery, ecology, natural phenomena, and the curiosity-driven study of living systems. Strong fits include: wildlife biology and species research, ecology studies and biodiversity findings, watershed and salmon research relevant to BC, astronomy and space science, new species discoveries, citizen science projects, natural history stories, wildfire science and forest ecology, climate science findings (not just policy), geology, evolution, and deep-time Earth stories, and any scientific research grounded in BC or Cariboo landscapes and ecosystems. Prefer articles that convey genuine curiosity and discovery — the 'how' and 'why' of the natural world. Score 70–90 for: prehistoric life and palaeontology (ancient oceans, Cretaceous ecology, deep-time species), new species discoveries in ocean or remote environments, deep-sea biology, evolutionary biology findings, natural history stories with a strong sense of wonder, and field research grounded in BC ecosystems. Penalise (score 0–30): consumer health and pharmaceutical research without ecology or natural-world context; pure policy and advocacy news; technology business stories without a science or ecology angle; human interest and viral news without scientific substance; geopolitical and crime news. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The James Webb Space Telescope has revealed surprising changes in the rings around Chariklo, a small object orbiting between Saturn and Uranus. Over just a few years, its inner ring became more opaque while its outer ring became less opaque. The results suggest that rings around small Solar System bodies may be much more dynamic than scientists previously believed. What is causing the changes remains a mystery.

items.title: [Fast Company] Raising kids has gotten so expensive, parents are turning to an unexpected lifeline
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

More than 3 in 4 parents say relying on Boomer grandparents is essential to afford raising kids

Raising children is becoming more and more costly, and modern parents are feeling the strain. Now, according to one new report, grown adults with children are relying on their own parents in high numbers.

The data comes from a survey of 2,500 U.S. adults by the global market research company Ipsos for the 2026 BMO Real Financial Progress Index. The research found that the large majority of parents in the U.S. believe that the cost of raising children is “out of control,” with 82% agreeing with the sentiment. Meanwhile, even nonparents are concerned about the cost of raising children, as 79% wonder how their peers can afford to have families. 

“Raising kids has always been a labor of love, but right now, it is also a major feat of financial engineering with families torn between spending on the urgent and the important,” Robin Growley, U.S. Head of Consumer Products, BMO, said in a news release.

Growley continued, “Whether you are budgeting for diapers or dorm rooms, the absolute best antidote to daily financial stress is a clear, actionable plan.” 

For many modern parents, part of the plan seems to be relying on their own boomer parents to afford raising their kids. In 2026, 76% of parents with children under 18 say that receiving financial support from extended family is necessary to afford opportunities for their children. Likewise, 37% of parents expect financial help from their parents or grandparents over the next year and plan to ask for it. 

Mostly, that group is getting help with daily living expenses. 47% of those who will ask for help say they will receive cash for their everyday needs. 43% say the help will come in the form of free childcare, provided by grandparents, or help with the costs of childcare. 26% say their family is helping financially by putting away funds for the future for their children.

The need for financial assistance isn’t due to the fact that modern parents are lazy or wildly over-spending. Mainly, it has to do with how quickly the cost of raising children has gone up drastically in recent years. According to a 2026 Lending Tree analysis, since 2023, the annual cost of raising a young child has skyrocketed by nearly 36%, coming to about $30,000 per year, or $300,000 over 18 years. 

Interestingly, while financial help from family may go a long way, there’s an emotional tax that comes with it. Those who live close to aging parents and receive help with the costs of raising children are more likely financially overwhelmed than those who don’t (74% as opposed to 57%).  

Growley noted that the numbers likely reflect the sandwich generation’s attunement with the fact that their parents raising children also realize their aging parents will soon be relying on them, too. “Having a grandparent help raise your kids can be one of life’s greatest gifts, but family caregiving is often a reciprocal arrangement—and it can be a lot when you’re already stretched thin,” Growley said.

items.title: [Fast Company] It took 2,977 drones to create this stunning 9/11 memorial show. Here’s how they pulled it off
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

To remember the lives of the 2,977 people killed in the 9/11 attacks 25 years ago, 2,977 drones were arranged in the shape of the original Minoru Yamasaki-designed World Trade Center at full architectural scale for a stunning temporary memorial. It took a lot of planning to make it work.

Called “2,977 Lights Over New York Harbor,” the commemorative public art installation on September 9 was sponsored by the New York Foundation for the Arts, and pulling it off required coordination with dozens of agencies. One of the biggest challenges was finding a suitable launch location.

“We need a lot of space to set the drones down,” Kyle Pivnick, vice president of Texas-based Sky Elements Drones, tells Fast Company, noting that thousands of hours went into finding the right path to bring the memorial to life.

The installation was produced by Sky Elements (which has put on professional drone shows for Formula 1 and Lollapalooza) in partnership with creative director Addison Mehr, Studio Drift, Ideko, designer Yan Paul Dubbelman, and artistic advisers Shigeru Ban and Dean Maltz, with input from 9/11 families, survivors, and first responders.

The installation’s creators needed about 12,000 square feet of flat, open-sky ground, which isn’t easy to find in New York City. Eventually, the U.S. Coast Guard agreed to let the creators use a parking lot at its recruitment office on the southern tip of Manhattan as the staging area.

The show was held for just one night, and it required flight restrictions so there would be no air traffic in the area, as well securing the ground below from people and moving vehicles, which is why it was held over the waterfront instead of the original World Trade Center location.

Using exactly 2,977 drones, one for each life lost at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and the United Airlines crash site in Pennsylvania on September 11, 2001, was foundational to the project. But that meant being deliberate about where to fill and add detail when re-creating the Twin Towers, Pivnick says.

“More drones would of course be better to give the towers more detail, but the choice to keep the drone count at 2,977 was paramount,” he says.

Drone shows are popular for advertising or entertainment events, but for “2,977 Lights Over New York Harbor,” the goal was to create an experience that was reverent and respectful.

The drones first appeared like two upward-swirling helixes before slowly rearranging into the shape of the towers. The helix shape was meant to recall the unbuilt proposal for a World Cultural Center memorial designed by Think that featured two open latticework towers.

By re-creating the towers as tall as they once stood, the installation gave a sense of scale and a feeling that’s larger than life. By using exactly 2,977 drones, the remembrance was poignant and personal.
